newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy govt confident "Euro-tax" will go through.
newsitem.headline: Italy govt confident "Euro-tax" will go through.

text.p: Italy's centre-left government, pushing ahead with its drive to prepare for European monetary union, said on Thursday it was confident a controversial "Euro-tax" would be approved by parliament.
"The Euro-tax is necessary to enter Europe. It will be approved and it will be approved well," Foreign Trade Minister Augusto Fantozzi told reporters in Vicenza.

At the same time, Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini told reporters that most of his small centrist Italian Renewal party's demands had been met after further discussions on a government amendment to the measure.
"The government amendment meets if not in full at least in large measure our proposals," Dini said.
Both men's comments marked a turnaround in the political climate on a day that had started with Dini reportedly rejecting the amendment as "completely insufficient".
The unpopular Euro-tax, designed to help Italy become a founder member of a single European currency in 1999, had exposed splits within the six-month-old government on Wednesday.
It had also been seen as a setback for Prime Minister Romano Prodi in the week in which he triumphantly took the lira back into Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM).

"With the ink on the signature of the lira's return to the ERM still wet and part of the budget still to be defined, it would be a tragedy if the prospect of political instability were to appear unexpectedly," La Stampa newspaper said in an editorial on Thursday.
Communist Refoundation, whose support will be crucial to secure final approval of the Euro-tax, had warned on Wednesday that "storm clouds" were gathering.
But Fantozzi, who is also a member of Dini's party, said he saw the government as "absolutely stable".

The Senate leaders of the parties in government said on Thursday they had reached a "broad agreement" on the main points of the Euro-tax but that more than 4,000 amendments tabled by the opposition remained a stumbling block.

The 12.5 trillion lire ($8.3 billion) Euro-tax is a key piece of Prodi's tough 1997 budget, which aims to prune 62.5 trillion lire off next year's deficit and spur Italy's hopes of joining economic and monetary union (EMU) from the start.
The 1997 budget -- minus the Euro-tax element -- has been passed in the lower Chamber of Deputies.

While ruffled feathers appeared to be smoothed over the Euro-tax, union leaders remained angry over the government's tentative steps to start reviewing a key pension reform deal a year earlier than scheduled.
Economic commentators say Italy needs to restructure its pension spending to help cut the state deficit and meet the strict criteria for single currency membership.
"A general strike is not a sport," Pietro Larizza, leader of the UIL union confederation, said. "But if the government touches pensions, it forces us into it."
Sergio D'Antoni, leader of the CISL confederation, promised Prodi a million people on the streets in Rome, as happened in 1994 over pensions in the biggest protest since World War Two.
